evals.prompt: I'm organizing DevCascadia, a 450-person community developer conference in a converted warehouse hall. We have 11 sponsor booths across three tiers. Lunch is a buffet at the far end of the hall and there's a lounge with couches near the entrance. My co-organizer wants to put all the sponsor tables in a side room off the main hall so the lunch queue doesn't get clogged, and to keep setup simple we figured we'd just let sponsors grab whichever table they like when they arrive - first come first served feels fairest. The floor plan goes to the printer in three weeks. How should we lay this out?
evals.expected_output: A floor layout that rejects the side room and the arrival free-for-all, sites booths on the existing food and lounge circulation path, works the review back from the print date, and routes safety dimensions to the venue.
expectations: Rejects moving the sponsor tables to a side room off the main hall
Recommends siting booths on the path attendees already take to the lunch buffet and the lounge, so foot traffic naturally passes them
Refuses first-come-first-served spot selection and requires a mapped floor with assigned positions before any sponsor arrives
Justifies the refusal by what self-selection rewards: whoever arrives earliest rather than whoever paid most, leaving the last sponsor in a dead corner with a legitimate complaint
Works the sign-off timeline back from the three-week print date rather than from the event date
Schedules the fire, egress and occupancy review before the plan is printed, not before doors open
States no universal aisle-width or egress figure and routes actual dimensions to the venue or its safety authority instead of quoting a number
Establishes what the signed floor plan already fixes (entrance, food service, where power and network reach) before placing booths
Flags that placing tables on a circulation corridor puts them on a route that may already be an egress path, so the narrowing must be checked before print
Presents the layout ranking as a default re-rankable by context, naming a condition that promotes an alternative (dedicated hall or booth count exceeding what the path holds)
Warns that the printed floor plan is the least reversible artifact produced, so late changes are the expensive failure
Assigns each tier a position class (which zone it draws from) as distinct from the specific spot, which is assigned later
Names the chosen traffic pattern explicitly rather than leaving it implied by the drawing

evals.prompt: Here's the sponsor benefits line we're about to publish for BeaconConf: 'Gold and Platinum sponsors receive a booth space with power and internet. Table provided.' Our tiers are Platinum at $12k, Gold at $7k, and Silver at $3.5k with no booth. Sponsors start asking logistics questions next week. Is this enough detail, or what am I missing?
evals.expected_output: A verdict that the line cannot ship as-is, plus a per-tier physical spec catalog with every field filled and the reasoning for why each blank becomes a morning-of failure.
expectations: States the published line is insufficient and must not go out as written
Prescribes or produces a tier-to-spec catalog with one row per booth-bearing tier
Covers all eight spec fields: footprint, furniture, position class, power, network, vertical limit, signage rule, and staffing
States footprint as a dimension in the venue's units, explicitly rejecting adjectives like 'a large table' as unbuildable for a sponsor planning a banner
Singles out the vertical limit and the signage rule as the fields organizers most often skip and regret
Flags that the power line must name who supplies the drop, who pays, and a request deadline
Flags that 'internet' must state wired versus wireless
Explains the cost of blanks: whoever is standing there at opening fills each one later, under time pressure, inconsistently
Connects the vertical limit to whether the booth behind can be seen, or the signage rule to keeping banners out of the aisle or fire lane
Gates tier differentiation on the shared-table versus full-table versus none axis rather than inventing a new differentiation axis
Marks any concrete dimensions or values it proposes as illustrative or self-set rather than presenting them as a published standard
Does not invent a foot-traffic or lead figure to justify the premium tier's position
Keeps repricing or redefining what the tiers promised out of scope, routing ladder changes to the sponsor-pricing side rather than rewriting packages here

evals.prompt: NorthStack Summit is a two-day conference with 16 sponsor booths. The venue gives us access from 06:00 on day one and needs the room clear by 21:00 on day two; they've confirmed there is no overnight storage and no access before 06:00. Our Platinum sponsor has a big modular stand that takes a while to assemble. I want to offer an overnight build the evening before as a premium perk, and to hit the 21:00 clear-out I'm planning to have sponsors start packing during the closing keynote, which ends at 17:30. Draft the load-in and load-out schedule.
evals.expected_output: A master schedule that deletes the overnight build outright, refuses teardown before the last session ends, gives the Platinum build a tiered or dedicated window, and writes rows as offsets from a fixed anchor with request deadlines included.
expectations: Removes the overnight pre-day build entirely given the venue's answer, rather than listing it as a demoted or discouraged option
States the reason for deletion: it is not a rung the organizer may choose against the venue's answer, and left visible it resurfaces as an unkeepable promise to a large sponsor
Refuses to let teardown start during the closing keynote; teardown never begins before the last session ends
Gives the teardown reason: packing noise lands inside the closing session and it silently breaks the floor-presence perk sponsors paid for
Solves the Platinum build with a tiered or dedicated earlier window instead of the overnight build
States that tiered windows beat the overnight build on both value and effort, so overnight is never the schedule answer here
Writes schedule rows as offsets from a fixed anchor such as the moment registration opens, not solely as clock times
Includes a request-deadline row (power and A/V requests close) as a published schedule row
Includes a shipping-window row stating the earliest date the venue accepts deliveries, or flags it as a venue fact to settle first
Includes a pre-doors floor-walk row checking aisles clear, nothing overhanging, every booth staffed, and every promised drop live
Includes an out-and-collected row stating when the room must be clear and what happens to anything left behind
Fits teardown between the 17:30 session end and the 21:00 clear-out rather than borrowing time from the program
Produces one master schedule for the whole floor and routes per-sponsor communication of it to the sponsor-fulfillment side rather than writing a schedule per sponsor

evals.prompt: Our venue contact for PortForward Conf says the room is provisioned at one power outlet per 10 attendees and the WiFi is sized for 2.5 devices per attendee across 600 attendees. We have 14 booths, and Gold sponsors were promised a power drop in their package. Can you work out a per-booth power and bandwidth allocation from those ratios? Also, one sponsor is planning a live cloud-gaming demo running over the venue WiFi.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to fabricate a conversion formula, replaced by the ask-the-venue process with a published per-tier inclusion list and request deadline, a needs-based drop count, and a WiFi fallback instruction for the demo sponsor.
expectations: Refuses to derive per-booth allocations from the aggregate attendee ratios
States why: attendee-density ratios and exhibitor load are different units with no formula bridging them, so any presented conversion is invented
Replaces the number with a process starting from asking the venue what a booth drop is, what it costs, and by when it must be requested
Routes the venue conversation through the organizers, who set expectations with venue staff
Publishes per tier what is included versus what must be requested
States the power request deadline as a published schedule row, not a sentence in an email
Counts booths that actually need a drop instead of provisioning all 14, distinguishing a laptop-and-banner table from a demo rig
Treats the WiFi inclusion as a commercial statement about billing, not a capacity or throughput promise
Tells the cloud-gaming demo sponsor to bring their own connectivity fallback rather than relying on venue WiFi
Asks or states whether wired connectivity is available at all as part of the per-tier network spec
Raises electrical safety sign-off: what supervision the venue requires and who is permitted to run a drop
Does not state a universal amperage, wattage or bandwidth threshold as if one existed

evals.prompt: Second edition of MergeConf coming up. Last year the four booths along the back wall told us basically nobody came by, and this year our biggest sponsor is asking what the premium corner spot near the entrance is actually worth - they want numbers on foot traffic or leads to justify paying for the upgrade. What do I tell them, and how do I fix the back-wall problem?
evals.expected_output: An honest refusal to quote position-value figures with the reason, a layout rework that puts every booth on a circulating path, and a measurement plan built on asking sponsors rather than inferring.
expectations: Refuses to quote a booth-position-to-lead or foot-traffic figure to the sponsor
States why: no usable measurement exists and what circulates is marketing material from companies selling booth displays, not developer-conference data
Recommends describing the position honestly - on the main circulation path or off a spur - and letting the sponsor judge the upgrade
Treats the dead-booth count as the number that judges the layout choice, collected by asking sponsors rather than inferred from observation
Diagnoses the back wall as a layout failure (booths off the circulation path) rather than a sponsor-effort failure
Proposes re-siting so no booth sits off a spur: booths on the food or hangout path, or a perimeter loop with one circulating route
Notes the perimeter-loop property that position barely matters, which is what makes an allocation easiest to defend to a sponsor who paid for a good spot
Aims the traffic mechanic at the booths the layout could not reach, not the booths already busy
Records last edition's dead spots and any hand-moved tables as the starting point for this edition's plan
Names a concrete floor-wide mechanic such as a passport or stamp card rather than generic promotion advice
Measures the mechanic by completions from attendees who were not already touring booths, not by raw cards returned
Does not promise the corner sponsor any lead uplift or dwell-time improvement as part of the pitch

evals.prompt: For StackFest we want attendees to visit every booth. My plan: a passport card, but a stamp only counts after the attendee has a proper conversation or watches a 2-minute demo, so sponsors get real engagement. A few sponsors also asked if they could just scan attendee badges to award the stamp so they get the contact list automatically. And our community manager suggested we skip all that and have each booth run its own raffle instead. Which way do we go?
evals.expected_output: A plain passport card with stamps given for showing up, the badge-scan variant reclassified as lead capture belonging downstream with a consent flow, and the per-booth raffle rejected as a floor mechanic with its reason.
expectations: Rejects requiring a conversation or demo before the stamp: the stamp is given for arriving, not for listening
Names the failure mode: conditioning the stamp converts a traffic mechanic into a forced pitch
Grounds the objection in the staffing guidance to send someone who can tell the story and participate with the community, not someone processing a queue
Rejects the badge-scanning variant as a floor traffic mechanic: once booths scan attendees it becomes lead capture with a consent flow attached
Routes the scanning question to the per-sponsor fulfillment side that owns lead capture, rather than adjudicating it here
Rejects the per-booth raffle as the floor-wide mechanic
Gives the raffle reason: its pull stays confined to the booth already running it and moves nobody toward the unreached booths
Routes the raffle to the per-sponsor fulfillment side as a lead-capture posture rather than banning it outright
Recommends the plain passport or stamp card as the default
States why the passport wins: it is the only option that makes every booth a required stop
States the scavenger-hunt promotion condition: a screen and someone to run it already exist, or the floor is too large for a card alone
Notes the plain card collects nothing beyond one winner's contact detail at claim time
Judges success by whether completed cards come from attendees who were not already engaged, not by completion volume

evals.prompt: Our Platinum sponsor at KernelDays paid $30k for a package that promised 'premium floor presence'. They want to bring a custom-built 4-meter stand and hang a wide banner from the ceiling truss above it. The venue is a commercial convention hall. The booth plan goes to print in 5 weeks. What do I need to line up?
evals.expected_output: A rigging and custom-structure plan gated on the venue's written permission, with the make-good exposure named, the fire review placed before the print run, and no invented safety dimensions.
expectations: Gates anything suspended from the ceiling or attached to the building on the venue's explicit rigging permission and required sign-off
Notes rigging often requires the venue's own contractor or crew, not the sponsor's or organizer's people
States both conditions for a custom top-tier structure: the package price promises floor presence a table cannot deliver, and the venue permits rigging - both required
Warns a rigging refusal the week of the event cannot be worked around: the structure simply does not go up
States the exposure: a sponsor whose package promised it is owed a make-good
Puts the rigging and labour questions to the venue in writing during negotiation, while leverage still exists, not after signature
Requires a vertical limit and signage rule in the tier spec covering the 4-meter stand, tied to whether the booth behind it stays visible
Schedules the fire and egress review before the 5-week print date, not before doors open
Works the approval timeline back from the print date as the anchor
Does not quote a universal height, aisle-width or egress number; routes dimensions to the venue and its jurisdiction
Keeps the custom structure to the top tier only, with standard table specs below, rather than opening bespoke builds to every sponsor
Checks venue-imposed labour rules for load-in and dock work, noting they cannot be renegotiated mid-setup

evals.prompt: We've signed 14 sponsors for CloudRidge Summit. Build me a tracking spreadsheet with a row per sponsor - payment received, booth staged, power drop confirmed, questions answered - and while you're at it, draft a reply to Vantiq Systems, who emailed asking how to ship their crates to the venue.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build the per-sponsor matrix inside floor design, replaced by the once-per-edition generic floor brief, with shipping answered at brief level for all sponsors and per-sponsor execution routed downstream.
expectations: Declines to build the per-sponsor tracking matrix as part of designing the floor
Routes per-sponsor execution - tracking, staging, payment gating, individual FAQ replies - to the sponsor-fulfillment side
Offers the once-per-edition generic floor brief as the deliverable instead
Names the brief's contents: the master schedule, the tier spec catalog, staffing and conduct provisioning rules, and a named contact
States the split explicitly: this work designs the floor once per edition; execution happens per signed sponsor downstream
Answers the shipping question at brief level - published shipping window, venue address and routing, fees - for all sponsors rather than as a one-off reply to Vantiq
Applies the routing pattern for sponsor questions: publish what is fixed, and name the person for everything else
Treats payment gating as a downstream concern, not a column tracked in this deliverable
Flags the earliest date the venue accepts deliveries as a venue fact to settle before the shipping row can be published
Does not quietly produce the requested spreadsheet anyway alongside the refusal

evals.prompt: Writing the booth rules for OpenGrid Conf. Three questions: how many staff should each sponsor bring? One sponsor wants to fly in six sales reps to badge-scan everyone who walks past. Do booth staff need badges themselves? And at our sister event last month, a sponsor's team showed up in branded swimsuits - if that happens here, what fine do we impose?
evals.expected_output: Provisioning rules only: a coverage obligation with a stated maximum, credentialed booth staff, the attire standard published before booking, and the sanction question refused and routed to the incident pipeline.
expectations: States staffing as a coverage obligation - the booth staffed the whole time the floor is open with a named person per shift - and lets the sponsor size the rota
States a maximum headcount as well as a minimum, because an over-staffed booth crowds the aisle it fronts
Advises sending someone who can tell the company's story and participate with the community, over reps trained to qualify or process a queue
Requires credentials that identify booth staff as booth staff
Gives the credential reason: a conduct policy that binds sponsor staff needs sponsor staff to be identifiable on the floor
Carries the attire standard - no sexualized clothing, uniforms, costumes or environments, per the standard conduct-code clause - as a provisioning line published before anyone books a stand
Refuses to set a fine or sanction: adjudication, sanctions and ejection are outside this design's remit
Routes any actual incident to the code-of-conduct incident pipeline the moment it stops being a provisioning question
Names one organizer on duty for the floor and tells every sponsor who it is
Explains the coverage rule's purpose: an unstaffed booth becomes a dead spot in the middle of the traffic pattern the floor was designed around
Distinguishes provisioning set before the floor opens from enforcement during the event
Does not draft a sanctions ladder or ejection procedure as part of the booth rules

evals.prompt: ByteHarbor Days: 300 developers, one big room. All 8 sponsors bought the exact same $4k package with identical benefits. I saw a conference where everything radiated out from a rented barista cart in the middle of the floor and it looked amazing - thinking of renting an espresso cart as our centerpiece, plus a premium zone near it for the sponsors we like most. Worth it?
evals.expected_output: The rented centerpiece declined with the promotion condition stated, the premium zone deleted because identical packages sold no differentiation, one spec for all eight booths, and circulation-path siting as the default for one room.
expectations: Advises against building the floor around a rented centerpiece: the hub layout is only promoted when a draw already exists for other reasons
States the reasoning: the central draw is programming that must be scheduled and staffed, its value never covers its effort, and the spoke ends starve anyway
Deletes the premium zone from the options given identical packages, rather than merely deprioritizing it
States why zoning is deleted: it would encode a distinction the packages never made, and every sponsor correctly reads it as arbitrary
Flags allocating good spots to 'the sponsors we like most' as indefensible when no tier sold position
Recommends one written spec applied to all 8 booths, since the ladder sold no floor differentiation
Defaults to siting the tables on the food or hangout circulation path for a single-room floor
Routes any genuine desire for tier differentiation to the package-ladder side rather than inventing floor differentiation here
Presents the layout ordering as a default re-ranked by this event's context: single room, existing assets, effort ceiling
Still requires a mapped floor with assigned spots even with identical specs - no arrival free-for-all
Keeps the full spec fields (dimension, height limit, signage rule) even for the single shared spec instead of 'a table will be provided'
